text: Ten years, handed down in 1934, and the task is to make that arithmetic felt rather than announced. Die Verlobte follows a woman convicted of antifascist activity into a prison where political prisoners are a small minority, which means her daily company is women jailed for everything else. Günther Rücker gives the story 105 minutes and spends them on the mechanics of endurance: work details, letters, the calendar as an instrument. The engagement that holds her together is less consolation than discipline, maintained across a wall and on a schedule other people set. The Crystal Globe went to it. What keeps the attention is the arithmetic itself — how a sentence gets served hour by hour, by a prisoner who can only take a decade a day at a time.

A group can talk one of its members out of almost anything, including an objection they were sure of five minutes earlier. Involuntary runs several unrelated stories at once, each hinged on one decision: to insist, or to weigh what insisting will cost and let it go. The listings say comedy and drama, and both hold, because social embarrassment plays as farce while it is happening and as damage afterwards. Ninety-eight minutes, Swedish dialogue, no plot to resolve — only pressure applied to people who would rather be agreeable than correct. The FLM survey of Swedish film keeps it on the list, and Ruben Östlund's later work has sent viewers back to it. What it notices is ordinary and hard to unsee afterwards: how often the person who ends up ashamed is not the one who did anything wrong.

The shop goes first, then the household, then the children. Ingeborg Holm runs 108 minutes and gives most of them to something unglamorous: the paperwork by which a widowed shopkeeper, bankrupt after her husband's illness, becomes a ward of poor relief while her three children are placed with other families. Victor Sjöström films the procedure — signatures, ledgers, the distance between a workhouse and a foster home measured in permissions rather than kilometres. The antagonist, if the word applies at all, is a relief system doing exactly what it was built to do. A mother wanting to see her children is not offered here as sentiment but as an administrative matter, and the steadiness with which a film from 1913 treats it as such is what still stings.

Three women wait out the last hours before labour in a Stockholm ward while the newspapers fill with a war that has just started. Loving Couples treats the waiting as licence to travel: childhoods and courtships arrive in pieces, so memory rather than chronology gives the film its order, and the hospital stays the one fixed point. Mai Zetterling is interested in what was done to these three before they got here — households, arrangements, men — and in how little of it they chose. Two hours, and the frankness is structural rather than shocking; bodies are the subject, not a figure of speech. Swedish critics have kept it on the FLM list of the country's best. The account it gives of how a woman is prepared for the position she is about to occupy is not a flattering one.

A robbery leaves two brothers holding a hostage of noble blood, which is a windfall and a death sentence in the same breath. Mikolás and Adam belong to a clan that lives by raiding, so the German king's anger is now only a question of timing; the errand that follows, bargaining with the neighbour Lazar for a defence pact, fails, and Mikolás answers the refusal by carrying off Lazar's daughter on the eve of her initiation as a nun. František Vláčil takes 166 minutes over this, and the length is the argument: the medieval world here is weather and mud and hunger, faith held with the same heat as a grudge. Marketa Lazarová is on the TSPDT thousand and it is not an easy sit. It asks for attention to loyalties that have no modern equivalent, and declines to translate them into ours.

Most of it happens at gates and counters, where a woman asks after her husband and is told to try elsewhere. Domingos has been taken by the Portuguese secret police for his part in an Angolan liberation movement, and Sarah Maldoror builds the film around his wife's walking rather than his cell: one prison station, then the next, the same question put to men with no reason to answer it. Colonial administration appears here as a series of doors, and the people behind them as bored rather than monstrous — the harder observation, and the more useful one. Lingala dialogue, 102 minutes, a shape borrowed from errands instead of plot. The TSPDT thousand lists it, though the reason to watch is plainer than that: someone has to go and ask, again, and the asking is the film.

Two men do paperwork in parallel, and one of them is preparing to shoot the president of France. The generals who hire the assassin known as the Jackal are disgruntled soldiers with money to spend; the gendarme sent after him has files, a telephone, and time, and Fred Zinnemann gives both sides the same unexcited attention across 143 minutes. Nothing in it is hectic. The Academy's editing award went to the one element the film could not survive without: a rhythm that keeps two separate schedules legible while they close on each other. Made in English about a French crisis, it holds because it treats killing a head of state as a job with logistics — travel, cover, patience, a story that has to survive one bored official. Competence observed closely is a durable pleasure, and here there are two sets of it.

Pride is this family's chief asset, and keeping it costs more than it is worth. Sway gives 120 minutes to a household whose members have agreed, without ever discussing it, on which things get said aloud. The listings file it under drama and crime, and the order is right: the interest lies less in what was done than in the pressure that follows, when relatives have to decide whose version of events they are willing to support. Miwa Nishikawa works at the scale of manners — a tone of voice, a pause, an inherited politeness that functions as coercion. Kinema Junpo's critics placed it among the best Japanese films of the decade. It is a patient film about people who have mistaken composure for loyalty, and it lets that mistake show itself in behaviour instead of announcing it in dialogue.

The premise is a friend's murder; nearly everything after it plays as a comedy of manners. Axel Foley is a Detroit street cop with a loose relationship to procedure, and Beverly Hills is a place where procedure is most of the local culture, so scene after scene becomes a negotiation about who is permitted to be standing where. Martin Brest keeps it to 105 minutes and lets the gunfire arrive late; the engine is the interval before anyone accepts that Foley is who he says he is. It ended up in the National Film Registry, an odd destination for a film whose funniest stretches consist of a man talking his way past a receptionist and plainly enjoying the work. The mystery is functional. The friction — accent, volume, class — is the film, and it has not gone stale.

Reluctance is the engine: an author who does not want her books filmed, sitting opposite the man determined to film them. Saving Mr. Banks turns that standoff into a haggle over specifics — what may be altered, what is not for sale — and keeps cutting from the meetings to the childhood P.L. Travers cannot stop returning to. The two halves pull against each other, which is the interesting part; the memories argue that the books were paid for in advance, while the negotiation insists that a story ends up belonging to whoever can put it on a screen. John Lee Hancock runs it at 126 minutes and lets the score carry a good deal of the persuasion, work the Academy recognised. It is finally about a bargain in which one party is charming and the other is right.
